html:
A full set of the Buddhist scriptures in Chinese, carved on more than 81,000 wooden printing blocks in Goryeo Korea in the 1200s. It is the oldest complete version of the East Asian Buddhist canon still in existence.

Goryeo had carved an earlier set in the 1000s, but invading Mongols burned it in 1232. The court, which had fled to Ganghwa Island, ordered a new set, hoping that the merit of the work would bring the Buddha's protection against the Mongol Empire. Carving took from about 1237 to 1248. The blocks are famous for their accuracy; the editors checked the texts carefully against other editions.

The blocks were moved in 1398 to the temple of Haeinsa in the mountains of the south. They are kept there in storage halls built in the 1400s, whose clever airflow has protected the wood from rot. The halls are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the blocks are listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World. Korea also gave the world Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with metal type.
